input: The Sherwood number is one of the most important dimensionless groups in the whole of mass transfer, and a proper understanding of it is essential for any student of the subject. In simple terms, the Sherwood number can be thought of as the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. In other words, it compares the rate at which a species is carried to or away from a surface by the movement of the fluid as a whole with the rate at which the same species would move by molecular diffusion alone. A value near 1 tells us that the two mechanisms are of comparable importance, so that the movement of the fluid adds very little to what diffusion would achieve on its own. At the other extreme, a large value tells us that convection dominates the transfer, and diffusion plays only a minor role, confined to a thin layer of fluid immediately next to the surface. The Sherwood number therefore provides a compact and convenient way of capturing the balance between these two fundamental mechanisms, and it plays a central role in the correlations that are used to predict mass-transfer coefficients in practice. Because the number is dimensionless, it allows results obtained under one set of conditions to be compared with results obtained under quite different conditions, and this is a large part of its appeal. Anything that strengthens the movement of the fluid relative to the movement of molecules will tend to push the value upwards, while anything that stills the fluid will bring it back down towards the diffusive case. It is, in short, a measure of which mechanism is in charge at the surface, and it should be read in that spirit whenever it is met.
target: The Sherwood number is a dimensionless group in mass transfer. It is defined as the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface: the rate at which the fluid motion delivers a species to the surface, or removes it, divided by the rate at which molecular diffusion alone moves the same species over the same length. A value near 1 means the two rates are comparable. Convection then adds little to diffusion, and the transfer at the surface is set by the diffusive step, as in a nearly stagnant fluid. A large value means convection is the larger rate by far. Diffusion is then confined to a thin layer of fluid at the surface, across which the concentration changes, and the resistance to transfer sits in that layer. Between the two cases the balance shifts continuously: as the fluid motion strengthens, the diffusive layer thins and the convective share of the transfer grows. Both rates in the ratio refer to the same surface and to the same driving difference in concentration. The group compares mechanisms, not sizes, and it has no units; two surfaces of different size in the same flow regime share the reading of the group even where their transfer rates differ. Anything that strengthens the fluid motion relative to molecular movement raises the group, and anything that stills the fluid lowers it towards the diffusive case. The group is used in correlations for the mass-transfer coefficient, where its value is stated as a function of the flow and the fluid properties; the definition above is what every such correlation reports, a comparison of the two transfer rates at the surface. Read the group as a comparison before reading it as a number: it states which mechanism sets the pace at the surface, and the correlations built on it inherit that reading.
